items.title: Appmotel
items.text: A no-frills PaaS (Platform as a Service) system using ubiquitous components like systemd, GitHub, and Traefik.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Appmotel is a minimalist PaaS that makes deploying and managing web applications as simple as a single command. Deploy Python, Node.js, and Go applications with automatic HTTPS, health checks, rate limiting, and seamless updates—all managed through systemd user services and Traefik reverse proxy.

Key Philosophy: - Use battle-tested, ubiquitous tools (systemd, Traefik, GitHub) - No complex orchestration or containers required - Simple, transparent operation - Easily auditable Bash scripts

items.title: ⚠️ Sysadmins: read this first, app isolation
items.text:
By default, all apps run as the same Linux user, appmotel. Every app can read the files of every other app, including their .env files with passwords and API keys. If one app has a security hole, an attacker can read the secrets of all apps on the server.

Use isolated apps for any app that holds secrets, or that you do not fully trust:

appmo add --isolated myapp user/repo      # new app, runs as its own user a-myapp
appmo isolate myapp                       # move an existing app to its own user

An isolated app runs as its own Linux user a-<app>. It cannot read appmotel's files, the files of other apps, or the TLS keys, and it has no sudo rights. appmotel and the operator still control it with the same appmo commands. On the server, an isolated app can connect only to its own app port, not to the ports of other apps.

Read Isolated Apps before you use it: it explains what is protected, what is not, and how to upgrade an existing server.

items.title: 🚀 Core Features
items.text:
• One-Command Deploy: appmo add myapp https://github.com/user/repo main
  • Subfolder Deploy: Deploy from repository subfolders using GitHub tree URLs
  • Multi-Component Apps: Auto-detects and deploys frontend + backend as unified app
  • Automatic HTTPS: Let's Encrypt integration via Traefik with wildcard certificate support
  • Zero-Downtime Updates: Automatic backup and rollback on failure
  • Multi-Process Apps: Procfile support for apps requiring multiple processes
  • Auto-Deploy: Automatic git polling and deployment every 2 minutes

items.title: 🛡️ Security & Reliability
items.text:
• Rate Limiting: Configurable request rate limiting per app (default: 100 req/sec)
  • Health Checks: Automatic health monitoring with 30-second intervals
  • Resource Limits: CPU and memory limits per app (default: 512M memory, 100% CPU)
  • Automatic Backups: Every update creates a timestamped backup
  • SSL/TLS: Automatic HTTPS with Let's Encrypt or existing wildcard certificates
  • Isolated Apps: appmo add --isolated runs an app as its own Linux user (see Isolated Apps)

items.title: 🎯 Developer Experience
items.text:
• Simple CLI: Intuitive appmo command (also installed as appmotel) with shell completion
  • Environment Variables: .env file support with proper quote handling
  • Real-Time Logs: appmo logs <app> shows live application logs
  • Exec Commands: Run commands in app environment with appmo exec
  • Backup/Restore: One-command backup and restore functionality

items.title: 🔧 Supported Platforms
items.text:
• Python: Virtual environment setup with requirements.txt or pyproject.toml; a Python version asked for with PYTHON_VERSION (app .env), .python-version or requires-python is installed with uv
  • Node.js: Auto-builds Next.js static export and Vite+TypeScript apps
  • Go: Automatic build with go.mod (supports cmd/ directory structure)
  • Multi-Component: Frontend/backend in {component}/ or src/{component}/ directories
  • Multi-Process: Procfile support (web, worker, etc.)

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (or similar Linux distribution)
  • Root access for initial setup
  • Domain name with DNS configured (see DNS Configuration below)

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Step 1: System-level setup (as root)

Run this once to create the appmotel user, configure systemd services, and set up permissions:

curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dirkpetersen/appmotel/main/install.sh?$(date +%s)" | sudo bash

Step 2: User-level setup (as appmotel user)

Switch to the appmotel user and run the installation to download Traefik, install the CLI tool, and configure everything:

sudo su - appmotel
curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dirkpetersen/appmotel/main/install.sh?$(date +%s)" | bash

This installs everything under /home/appmotel and starts the necessary services.

Alternative: If you have the repository cloned locally, you can run sudo bash install.sh (Step 1) and bash install.sh (Step 2) from the repo directory instead.

Step 3: Allow people to use appmo (as root)

👉 Which group is right for a person? See the table Users and operators: who is who.

Step 1 creates two groups: appmotel-users for people who deploy apps, and appmotel-ops for the admins of appmotel itself. Members of appmotel-users may run the appmo command, and nothing else, as the appmotel user. They type appmo ... directly; sudo -u appmotel is not needed. Add each person once:

sudo usermod -aG appmotel-users joe

Joe must log in again, so that the new group is active. Then Joe can run:

appmo list
appmo add --isolated myapp joe/myrepo main

To remove the access again: sudo gpasswd -d joe appmotel-users.

An admin of appmotel goes into the operator group instead:

sudo usermod -aG appmotel-ops alice

⚠️ A member controls all apps, not only the apps that this person added. For example, appmo exec runs any command in any app, and appmo env shows its secrets. Add only people that you trust with every app on this server. Members get no root rights, and no shell as appmotel.

Who did what: every appmo command of a member is written to syslog with the real user name. Two records are kept:

journalctl -t appmo                      # from appmo:  user=joe as=appmotel cmd=appmo add --isolated myapp ...
journalctl _COMM=sudo | grep appmo       # from sudo:   joe : ... USER=appmotel ; COMMAND=/home/appmotel/.local/bin/appmo add ...

On systems that write syslog files, the same lines are in /var/log/auth.log (Debian, Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL).

items.title: Users and operators: who is who
items.text:
Think of appmotel as a building with many apartments, where each app is an apartment.

  • Users (the group appmotel-users) are like the front-desk staff. They use one tool, the appmo command, to move apps in and out, restart them and look at them. They cannot do anything else as appmotel. Every action is written to a log with their name.
  • Operators (the group appmotel-ops, and the user apps) are the caretakers. They have the master key: they can do anything as appmotel, also without appmo. For example, they can open a shell as appmotel, change the Traefik settings by hand or read the TLS keys. Only their appmo commands are logged in detail.
  • Operators can also read the whole system journal (journalctl, journalctl -t appmo). install.sh gives the group appmotel-ops a read ACL on /var/log/journal, so new members need no extra group. This needs a persistent journal (/var/log/journal must exist; Ubuntu has it). Users in appmotel-users see only their own journal; they use appmo logs <app> for app logs.
  • Root is the owner of the building and can do everything.
User Operator Add, update, restart, remove apps yes yes See and change the settings of every app yes (appmo exec, appmo env) yes Work as appmotel without appmo (shell, Traefik, TLS keys) no yes Everything logged with the person's name yes only appmo commands How to add a person sudo usermod -aG appmotel-users joe sudo usermod -aG appmotel-ops alice How to remove a person sudo gpasswd -d joe appmotel-users sudo gpasswd -d alice appmotel-ops

After a change, the person must log in again.

Important: a user can still reach every app, not only their own apps. appmotel has no "my apps only" right. So both roles are for people you trust. Make developers users, and make only the admins of appmotel itself operators.

Being a user does not make anyone an operator. A person in both groups is an operator.

More operators without the group: OPERATOR_USERS in /home/appmotel/.config/appmotel/.env (default apps) takes user names and other %groups, then run sudo bash install.sh. appmotel-ops is always added. OPERATOR_USERS="ALL" makes every account on the machine an operator; use it only where every login is trusted.

items.title: Upgrading an existing server
items.text:
appmo self-update updates the appmo command, Traefik and the configs, but it cannot change the sudo rules or create groups, because it does not run as root. After an upgrade that changes rights (for example the groups appmotel-users and appmotel-ops), run both parts, from a checkout of the new version:

sudo bash install.sh        # part 1 (root): groups and sudo rules
appmo self-update           # part 2: the new appmo, Traefik and configs

The order does not matter. Until part 2 is done, operators keep working, but members of appmotel-users are refused: they need the new appmo.

items.title: Deploy Your First App
items.text:
# Add and deploy an app
appmo add myapp https://github.com/username/myrepo main

# Or deploy from a subfolder (GitHub tree URL)
appmo add myapp https://github.com/username/myrepo/tree/main/apps/myapp

# Check status
appmo status myapp

# View logs
appmo logs myapp

# Your app is now live at: https://myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu

items.title: CLI Commands
items.text:
# Application Management
appmo add <app-name> <url|user/repo> [branch] # Deploy a new app
appmo add <app-name> <github-tree-url>        # Deploy from subfolder
appmo add --isolated <app-name> <url>         # Deploy as its own Linux user a-<app-name>
appmo isolate <app-name>                      # Move an existing app to its own user
appmo remove <app-name>                       # Remove an app (alias: rm)
appmo list                                    # List all apps (alias: ls)
appmo status [app-name]                       # Show app status

# App Control
appmo start <app-name>                        # Start an app
appmo stop <app-name>                         # Stop an app
appmo restart <app-name>                      # Restart an app
appmo update <app-name>                       # Update app (auto-backup & rollback)
appmo rollback <app-name> [backup-id]         # Back to the version before the last update, pinned
appmo unpin <app-name>                        # Let autopull update a rolled-back app again

# Updates & Automation
appmo check [app-name]                        # Check for updates (no deploy)
appmo autopull                                # Check all apps for updates and deploy

# Environment Management
appmo env <app-name>                          # Edit app's .env file (vim, mouse off for copy and paste)
appmo env <app-name> get KEY                  # Print one value
appmo env <app-name> set KEY VALUE            # Set one value (then appmo restart <app-name>)
printf '%s' "$SECRET" | appmo env <app-name> set KEY   # Value from stdin: not in the logs
appmo env <app-name> set < secrets.env        # Many KEY=VALUE lines from stdin (all or none)
appmo env <app-name> unset KEY                # Remove a variable

# Monitoring & Debugging
appmo logs <app-name> [lines]                 # View application logs (and scheduled jobs)
appmo logs <app-name> --since "1h ago" --grep 'ERROR|Traceback'   # Search; --follow to watch
appmo top [app-name...]                       # Memory, CPU time, restarts, disk per app
appmo certs                                   # TLS certificates and when they expire
appmo exec <app-name> <command>               # Run command in app environment

# Backup & Restore
appmo backup <app-name>                       # Create backup
appmo restore <app-name> [backup-id]          # Restore from backup
appmo backups <app-name>                      # List available backups (with their commit)
appmo backup-verify <app-name> [backup-id]    # Check a backup can be restored (default: newest)

# System Maintenance
appmo self-update                             # Update appmo CLI, Traefik, and configs

appmo rollback restores the newest backup of a different commit, which is the version from before the last update. It brings back both the code and the .env from that time, and reinstalls the dependencies. It backs up the current state first, so appmo restore <app> <id> can undo it (appmo backups marks that backup "state before a rollback"; a second appmo rollback skips it and goes one version further back). It then pins the app: autopull leaves it alone, because it would otherwise deploy the bad commit again within two minutes. The app is pinned even if the restore fails, so that autopull does not deploy over a half-restored app. appmo unpin (next autopull) or appmo update (now) follows the branch again. appmo status shows the pin; appmo isolate refuses a pinned app, because the isolated copy is deployed from the branch.

appmo backup-verify restores nothing. It checks that the code archive reads to the end, extracts to an intact git repository (git fsck) of the recorded commit, that the settings parse, and that the unit files and the Traefik route are in the backup.

items.title: Application Requirements
items.text:
Each app repository must contain:

1. .env file - Environment variables and configuration 

PORT=8000
APP_NAME="My Application"

# Optional: Resource limits
MEMORY_LIMIT=512M
CPU_QUOTA=100%

# Optional: Rate limiting
RATE_LIMIT_AVG=100
RATE_LIMIT_BURST=50
# DISABLE_RATE_LIMIT=true

# Optional: Health checks
HEALTH_CHECK_PATH=/health

2. install.sh - Installation/setup script (run on deploy and update) 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Installing dependencies..."
# Your installation commands here

3. Application entry point - One of: - Python: app.py or requirements.txt - Node.js: package.json with start script - Go: go.mod (builds to bin/ directory, supports cmd/ structure) - Procfile: For multi-process apps

items.title: Procfile Support
items.text:
For applications requiring multiple processes:

Procfile: 

web: python app.py
worker: celery -A tasks worker
scheduler: python scheduler.py

Each process gets its own systemd service: - appmotel-myapp-web - appmotel-myapp-worker - appmotel-myapp-scheduler

The web process receives the main port and is accessible via HTTPS.

items.title: Scheduled Jobs
items.text:
For periodic tasks, add a file appmo-schedule to the app folder. Each line is a systemd calendar expression, |, and a command:

# <when> | <command>   (runs in the app folder, with the app's .env and venv)
daily | python3 cleanup.py
*-*-* 02:30:00 | ./bin/report --email
Mon..Fri 08:00 | curl -fsS http://localhost:$PORT/tasks/digest
*:0/15 | python3 sync.py

appmo add, update, restore and rollback turn each line into a systemd timer appmotel-<app>.job-<n>. Missed runs (server off) run at the next boot. A job has the app's MEMORY_LIMIT and CPU_QUOTA, and is stopped after JOB_TIMEOUT (default 1h). Lines that do not parse are skipped with a warning; check an expression with systemd-analyze calendar '<when>'. appmo status lists the jobs with their next run, appmo logs includes their output, and appmo stop / start pause and resume them. Test a command first with appmo exec <app> <command>.

items.title: System Configuration
items.text:
Configure Appmotel via .env file in the project root:

# Base domain for applications
BASE_DOMAIN="apps.yourdomain.edu"

# Let's Encrypt settings
USE_LETSENCRYPT="yes"
LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL="admin@yourdomain.edu"
LETSENCRYPT_MODE="http"  # or "dns" for DNS-01 challenge

# AWS credentials (only for DNS-01 mode with Route53)
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="your-key"
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="your-secret"
AWS_REGION="us-west-2"

How the TLS certificate is chosen:

  1. A wildcard certificate for exactly *.BASE_DOMAIN in /etc/letsencrypt/live/ (for example one that a sysadmin issued with certbot) is used for all apps. Certificates for other domains are never used.
  2. Otherwise, with USE_LETSENCRYPT=yes, Traefik gets certificates from Let's Encrypt. With LETSENCRYPT_MODE="http" (port 80) it gets one certificate for each app, and with "dns" (Route53) one wildcard certificate for all apps. See TLS Certificates.

On a new install with no such wildcard certificate, install.sh sets USE_LETSENCRYPT=yes by itself when no other program uses port 80, and an active ufw or firewalld allows it. It cannot see outside firewalls (such as an AWS security group). If those block port 80, Traefik only logs failed Let's Encrypt attempts. LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL is optional; Let's Encrypt rejects example.com addresses.

items.title: Servers with more than one network card
items.text:
By default Traefik listens on ports 80 and 443 on all addresses of the server. If the server has a second network card, for example for a storage network, apps are then also reachable on that network. To listen on one address only, set it in /home/appmotel/.config/appmotel/.env:

APPMOTEL_BIND_IP="192.0.2.40"     # the IP of the primary network card

Then run appmo self-update. Traefik then listens only on 192.0.2.40:80 and 192.0.2.40:443. Use an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 address in brackets ([2001:db8::40]). An empty value (APPMOTEL_BIND_IP="") means all addresses again.

  • First install: the installer cannot know which card is the primary one, so it does not guess. Give the IP to the user part of the install: APPMOTEL_BIND_IP="192.0.2.40" bash install.sh. It is saved in the .env. If the server has more than one IP and none is set, the installer warns and lists the addresses.
  • Upgrades never undo a hand edit: if traefik.yaml was changed by hand to listen on one IP and the .env has no APPMOTEL_BIND_IP, install.sh and appmo self-update keep that IP and save it in the .env.
  • Your DNS records for BASE_DOMAIN must point to that IP (or to a public IP that is forwarded to it).
  • The app ports themselves are already closed to other networks: they only accept connections from the server itself (see Security Considerations).

items.title: Per-App Configuration
items.text:
Apps can override defaults in their .env file:

# Resource Limits
MEMORY_LIMIT=1G          # Max memory (default: 512M)
CPU_QUOTA=200%           # CPU quota (default: 100%)

# Rate Limiting
RATE_LIMIT_AVG=200       # Requests/sec average (default: 100)
RATE_LIMIT_BURST=100     # Burst requests (default: 50)
DISABLE_RATE_LIMIT=true  # Disable rate limiting

# Health Checks
HEALTH_CHECK_PATH=/api/health  # Health endpoint (default: /health)

# Crash loops: stop restarting after 5 starts in RESTART_WINDOW seconds (default
# 300). Unset (default): restart every 10 s forever. appmo restart starts it again.
RESTART_LIMIT=5
RESTART_WINDOW=300

# Scheduled jobs (appmo-schedule): stop a job after this long (default 1h)
JOB_TIMEOUT=2h

# Backups to keep (default 5)
BACKUP_RETENTION=5

# Chat webhook for this app (default: the global NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_URL)
NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.slack.com/services/...

RESTART_LIMIT and RESTART_WINDOW go into a systemd drop-in (appmotel-<app>.service.d/restart-limit.conf) that appmo start, restart, update and restore rewrite, so after a change run appmo restart <app>.

items.title: Notifications
items.text:
With NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_URL set, appmotel posts one line to that chat webhook (Slack format {"text": ...}, which Mattermost, Rocket.Chat and Google Chat accept too). It posts for a deploy (old → new commit), a failed update and its automatic rollback, an appmo rollback, a crash loop, and a TLS certificate that expires within TLS_EXPIRY_WARN_DAYS (default 14). Set it in ~/.config/appmotel/.env for all apps, or in an app's .env for that app. An isolated app has to set its own, because its user cannot read appmotel's .env.

A crash loop is a service that restarted 3 or more times between two autopull runs (2 minutes), or that systemd stopped restarting because of RESTART_LIMIT. Autopull logs it as an error and notifies at most once an hour per app. appmo status shows a crashed or failed service and its restart count.

items.title: DNS Configuration
items.text: Appmotel requires DNS to route traffic from your domain (e.g., apps.yourdomain.edu) to your deployed applications. Each app gets a unique subdomain like myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu.

items.title: Configuration Options
items.text: Choose the DNS configuration method that best fits your environment:

items.title: Option 1: AWS Route53 Automatic DNS (Best for AWS)
items.text:
When to use: - You're deploying on AWS EC2 - Your domain is hosted in Route53 - You want fully automatic DNS configuration

Setup: Use the install-aws.sh script which automatically: 1. Creates an EC2 instance with IAM role for Route53 access 2. Detects your hosted zone 3. Creates wildcard DNS records (*.apps.yourdomain.edu) 4. Configures DNS-01 challenge for wildcard SSL certificates

bash install-aws.sh [--type t4g.small] [--region us-west-2] [--hosted-zone ZONE_ID]
bash install-aws.sh --hosted-zone ZONE_ID --subdomain apps   # BASE_DOMAIN=apps.<zone>

It uploads this checkout and runs both parts of install.sh. It never replaces existing DNS records unless you give --force. Use --subdomain if the zone is also used for other things: then the records are appmotel.apps.<zone> and *.apps.<zone>, and the zone's own records stay as they are. If your AWS user may not read IAM, an admin must create the role appmotel-route53-role and the instance profile appmotel-instance-profile once.

Advantages: - ✅ Fully automatic DNS and SSL setup - ✅ No manual DNS configuration required - ✅ Wildcard certificates via DNS-01 challenge - ✅ IAM role authentication (no AWS keys on server)

Disadvantages: - ⚠️ AWS-specific (requires Route53 hosted zone) - ⚠️ Requires AWS account with Route53 access

items.title: Option 2: Wildcard A Record (Recommended)
items.text:
When to use: - You control the DNS zone for your domain - Your DNS provider supports wildcard records - You want a simple, maintenance-free solution

Setup: Add a wildcard A record in your DNS zone:

*.apps.yourdomain.edu.  IN  A  203.0.113.10

This routes ALL subdomains under apps.yourdomain.edu to your server.

Advantages: - ✅ New apps automatically work without DNS updates - ✅ Simple to configure (single DNS record) - ✅ No additional software required - ✅ Best for most use cases

Disadvantages: - ⚠️ Not all DNS providers support wildcards - ⚠️ All subdomains point to same IP (not ideal for split deployments)

items.title: Option 3: Individual CNAME or A Records (Fallback)
items.text:
When to use: - Your DNS provider doesn't support wildcard records - You need explicit control over each subdomain - You have a small number of apps

Setup: For each app, add a DNS record:

Option 3a: A Record (points directly to IP) 

myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu.  IN  A  203.0.113.10

Option 3b: CNAME Record (points to another hostname) 

myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu.  IN  CNAME  server.yourdomain.edu.

Advantages: - ✅ Works with all DNS providers - ✅ Explicit control over each app's DNS - ✅ Can point different apps to different servers

Disadvantages: - ⚠️ Requires manual DNS update for EVERY new app - ⚠️ More maintenance overhead - ⚠️ DNS propagation delay for new apps

items.title: Option 4: On-Premises with Route53 DNS-01
items.text:
Status: LETSENCRYPT_MODE="dns" works with Route53 and gets one wildcard certificate for all apps. Automatic setup for on-premises servers is planned.

When to use: - Your server is on-premises or in a non-AWS datacenter - Port 80 is blocked by firewall or not exposed to the internet - Your domain is hosted in AWS Route53 - You want automatic wildcard SSL certificates without HTTP-01 challenge

Why this matters:

Let's Encrypt offers two main challenge types for certificate validation: - HTTP-01: Requires port 80 open to the internet (not always possible on-premises) - DNS-01: Validates via DNS TXT records (works behind firewalls, supports wildcards)

With Route53 DNS-01 support, Traefik can: 1. Automatically create DNS TXT records in Route53 for certificate validation 2. Obtain and renew wildcard certificates (*.apps.yourdomain.edu) 3. Work entirely behind a firewall with no inbound port 80 required 4. Only requires outbound HTTPS access to Let's Encrypt and Route53 APIs

Setup:

# Install appmotel on your on-premises server
sudo bash install.sh
sudo su - appmotel
bash install.sh

# Configure Route53 DNS-01 in ~/.config/appmotel/.env
BASE_DOMAIN="apps.yourdomain.edu"
USE_LETSENCRYPT="yes"
LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL="admin@yourdomain.edu"
LETSENCRYPT_MODE="dns"              # Use DNS-01 challenge
AWS_HOSTED_ZONE_ID="Z1234567890"    # Your Route53 hosted zone ID
AWS_REGION="us-east-1"

# AWS credentials (if not using instance profile)
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="AKIA..."
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="..."

Advantages: - ✅ Works behind firewalls (no inbound port 80 needed) - ✅ Automatic wildcard certificates for all apps - ✅ Certificate renewal without service interruption - ✅ On-premises servers can use cloud DNS - ✅ Single certificate covers all *.apps.yourdomain.edu subdomains

Requirements: - AWS account with Route53 hosted zone - IAM credentials with Route53 permissions (or EC2 instance role if on AWS) - Outbound HTTPS access to Let's Encrypt and AWS APIs - Wildcard A record in Route53 pointing to your server's public IP

Network Requirements: 

Outbound only (no inbound ports required):
├── HTTPS (443) → acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org (Let's Encrypt API)
├── HTTPS (443) → route53.amazonaws.com (Route53 API)
└── HTTPS (443) → sts.amazonaws.com (AWS STS for auth)

Set the values above, then run appmo self-update. See TLS Certificates for the IAM permissions and how to switch a running server.

items.title: DNS Configuration Workflow
items.text:
When you add a new app, Appmotel automatically displays DNS configuration guidance if the app URL is not yet accessible:

$ appmo add myapp https://github.com/username/myrepo main

App 'myapp' added successfully
URL: https://myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu

DNS Configuration Required:

   Configure DNS to route traffic to this app. Choose one option:

   Option 1 (Recommended): Wildcard A record
     *.apps.yourdomain.edu IN A 203.0.113.10
     → All subdomains automatically route to this server

   Option 2: Individual A record
     myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu IN A 203.0.113.10
     → Requires manual DNS update for each new app

Note: If you deployed via install-aws.sh with Route53, DNS is configured automatically and you won't see this message.

items.title: Testing DNS Configuration
items.text:
After configuring DNS, verify it's working:

# Test DNS resolution
dig myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu

# Test HTTP connectivity (should redirect to HTTPS)
curl -v http://myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu

# Test HTTPS connectivity
curl -v https://myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu

# Check certificate
openssl s_client -connect myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu:443 -servername myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu </dev/null 2>&1 | grep "subject="

items.title: Troubleshooting DNS Issues
items.text:
DNS not resolving: - Check DNS propagation: dig myapp.apps.yourdomain.edu - Wait for DNS TTL to expire (usually 300-3600 seconds) - Verify your DNS records in your provider's control panel

Certificate errors: - Ensure Let's Encrypt is enabled in ~/.config/appmotel/.env - Check Traefik logs: sudo journalctl -u traefik-appmotel -f - Verify DNS is resolving correctly before attempting HTTPS

404 errors on HTTPS: - Verify app is running: appmo status myapp - Check Traefik dynamic config: cat ~/.config/traefik/dynamic/myapp.yaml - Review app logs: appmo logs myapp

├── .local/

items.title: Automatic Deployment (Autopull)
items.text: Appmotel automatically checks all deployed apps for updates every 2 minutes using a systemd timer. When updates are detected, apps are automatically redeployed.

items.title: How It Works
items.text:
1. Systemd Timer: appmotel-autopull.timer runs every 2 minutes
  2. Git Polling: The appmo-autopull script checks each app for updates
  3. Automatic Deploy: When changes are found, appmo update <app> runs automatically
  4. Rollback on Failure: If deployment fails, the previous version is automatically restored
  5. Pinned apps are skipped: after appmo rollback, an app is not updated until appmo unpin or appmo update
  6. Health: each run reports crash loops, and once a day expiring TLS certificates (see Notifications)

items.title: Security Considerations
items.text:
• By default all apps run as the appmotel user and can read each other's files. Use appmo add --isolated or appmo isolate to run an app as its own user (see Isolated Apps)
  • appmotel's config and data folders are mode 700, .env files mode 600
  • Traefik runs with minimal privileges using CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
  • App ports (10001-59999) accept new connections only from the server itself. Many apps listen on all addresses (for example Flask with host='0.0.0.0'), so without this rule they could be reached past Traefik, also from a second network. sudo bash install.sh installs the rule as appmotel-firewall.service (an nftables table inet appmotel). Replies to the server's own outgoing connections are not affected. On the server itself, isolated app users may open connections only to their own app port; Traefik (appmotel), root and other users are not affected. To check: sudo nft list table inet appmotel. An admin who disables the service (sudo systemctl disable --now appmotel-firewall) keeps it disabled on reinstall.
  • Apps are isolated by systemd resource limits
  • HTTPS enforced via automatic redirect
  • Rate limiting prevents abuse
  • Regular backups enable quick recovery

items.title: Auto-Debug: Automated Error Detection and GitHub Issue Filing
items.text: Appmotel can automatically detect runtime errors in deployed apps, analyze them with Claude Code, and file GitHub issues against the app's source repository.

items.title: How It Works
items.text:
The auto-debug system runs as part of the autopull cycle (every 2 minutes via appmotel-autopull.timer). For each deployed app, check_app_errors() in bin/appmo performs these steps:

  1. Opt-out check — Skips apps with AUTO_DEBUG=no in their .env
  2. Cooldown check — Skips apps that had an issue filed in the last 24 hours (timestamp in ~/.config/appmotel/<app>/.auto-debug-cooldown)
  3. Log scan — Reads the last 3 minutes of journalctl --user -u appmotel-<app> output
  4. Error detection — Searches for patterns: ERROR, CRITICAL, EXCEPTION, TRACEBACK, FATAL, PANIC:, UnhandledPromise
  5. Prerequisite check — Verifies that claude (Claude Code CLI) and gh (GitHub CLI, authenticated) are both available
  6. Claude analysis — Pipes the logs to claude -p with a structured prompt requesting TITLE:, CAUSE:, and FIX: sections
  7. Issue filing — Uses gh issue create to file against the app's GITHUB_URL (from metadata.conf), including the error excerpt, Claude's analysis, and full logs in a collapsible section
  8. Cooldown stamp — Writes the current Unix timestamp to the cooldown file

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: Both tools must be installed and configured on the appmotel server:

items.title: Claude Code CLI
items.text:
# Install (see https://claude.ai/code)
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
# Or via curl installer — check the official docs for current instructions

items.title: GitHub CLI
items.text:
# Install
sudo apt install gh          # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo dnf install gh          # RHEL/Amazon Linux

# Authenticate (required — must have access to file issues on app repos)
gh auth login

Verify both: 

command -v claude && echo "claude OK"
gh auth status

items.title: Global (default: enabled)
items.text: Auto-debug is enabled by default for all apps. No global configuration is needed — it activates automatically when both claude and gh are available. If either tool is missing, it silently skips with an informational log message.

items.title: Per-App Opt-Out
items.text:
Add to the app's .env file:

AUTO_DEBUG=no

Edit via: appmo env <app-name>

items.title: Cooldown Period
items.text:
The default cooldown is 24 hours (86400 seconds), hardcoded in check_app_errors(). After filing an issue for an app, no further issues will be filed for that app until the cooldown expires.

The cooldown file is stored at: 

~/.config/appmotel/<app>/.auto-debug-cooldown

To force a re-check (e.g., after deploying a fix), delete the cooldown file: 

rm ~/.config/appmotel/<app>/.auto-debug-cooldown

items.title: Error Detection Patterns
items.text:
The log scan uses case-insensitive grep with these patterns:

Pattern Catches ERROR Python logging, generic frameworks, Java CRITICAL Python logging critical level EXCEPTION Python/Java exception messages TRACEBACK Python Traceback (most recent call last): FATAL Go log.Fatal, generic fatal errors PANIC: Go panic: runtime errors UnhandledPromise Node.js UnhandledPromiseRejectionWarning

items.title: GitHub Issue Format
items.text:
Filed issues include:

  • Title: [appmotel] <Claude's one-line summary>
  • Body:
  • Server hostname and UTC timestamp
  • Error excerpt (just the matched error lines)
  • Claude Code analysis (cause + suggested fix)
  • Full recent logs in a collapsible <details> block
  • Footer with opt-out instructions

items.title: Where the code lives
items.text:
• bin/appmo — check_app_errors() (lines ~3133-3292): The main function
  • bin/appmo — cmd_autopull(): Calls check_app_errors "${app_name}" at the end of each app's update-check iteration

items.title: Metadata dependency
items.text: The function reads GITHUB_URL from ~/.config/appmotel/<app>/metadata.conf (written by save_app_metadata() during appmo add). This is the target repo for gh issue create. If GITHUB_URL is missing, auto-debug is skipped for that app.

items.title: Deduplication strategy
items.text: A simple timestamp-based cooldown file. The system does not track error fingerprints — if the same error recurs after the cooldown expires, a new issue will be filed. This is intentional: recurring errors after 24 hours likely indicate the issue wasn't resolved.

items.title: Failure modes
items.text:
All failures are non-fatal (the function returns 0):

Condition Behavior No errors in logs Silent return claude not installed Logs: "auto-debug requires Claude Code CLI" gh not installed Logs: "auto-debug requires the GitHub CLI" gh not authenticated Logs: "auto-debug requires 'gh auth login'" No GITHUB_URL in metadata Logs warning, skips Claude returns empty output Logs warning, skips gh issue create fails Logs warning, does NOT write cooldown (will retry next cycle)

items.title: Security considerations
items.text:
• Claude Code runs in non-interactive print mode (-p) — no filesystem access, no code execution
  • The gh CLI must be pre-authenticated; auto-debug does not store or handle any credentials
  • Log content is sent to Claude's API for analysis; ensure no secrets are logged by your apps
  • Issues are filed under the authenticated GitHub user's identity

items.title: Development Environment Setup
items.text: This document explains the execution model and permission structure for Appmotel.

items.title: Execution Model Overview
items.text:
Appmotel uses a three-tier permission delegation model:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIER 1: Operator User (e.g., "apps")                           │
│  - Runs Claude Code or other automation tools                   │
│  - Has full control over the appmotel user                      │
│  - Cannot directly run root commands                            │
└───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                        │ sudo -u appmotel
                        ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIER 2: Service User ("appmotel")                              │
│  - Owns all Appmotel files and services                         │
│  - Manages user-level systemd services (no root needed)         │
│  - Has LIMITED sudo access for specific systemctl commands      │
└───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                        │ sudo /bin/systemctl (limited)
                        ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIER 3: Root (strictly limited)                                │
│  - Only for Traefik service management                          │
│  - No general root access granted                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

items.title: Sudoers Configuration
items.text:
Location: /etc/sudoers.d/appmotel

# Allow operator user to switch to appmotel interactively
apps ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/su - appmotel

# Allow operator user to run any command as appmotel (for automation)
apps ALL=(appmotel) NOPASSWD: ALL

# Allow appmotel to manage ONLY the Traefik system service
appmotel ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart traefik-appmotel, /bin/systemctl stop traefik-appmotel, /bin/systemctl start traefik-appmotel, /bin/systemctl status traefik-appmotel

# Allow appmotel to view ONLY traefik-appmotel logs with any journalctl options
appmotel ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/journalctl -u traefik-appmotel, /usr/bin/journalctl -u traefik-appmotel *

# Note: appmotel user does NOT need sudo access for Traefik config changes
# Traefik automatically reloads dynamic configuration changes

items.title: Line-by-Line Explanation
items.text: Line Purpose apps ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/su - appmotel Allows operator user to switch to appmotel interactively apps ALL=(appmotel) NOPASSWD: ALL Allows operator user to run any command as appmotel (for automation) appmotel ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl ... Allows appmotel to manage Traefik system service appmotel ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/journalctl -u traefik-appmotel* Allows appmotel to view full Traefik logs for debugging

items.title: Managing Traefik Service
items.text:
The Traefik service runs as a system-level service (not user-level) because it needs to bind to privileged ports 80 and 443.

Correct way to manage Traefik: 

# From operator user (apps), execute as appmotel, then use sudo
sudo -u appmotel sudo systemctl start traefik-appmotel
sudo -u appmotel sudo systemctl stop traefik-appmotel
sudo -u appmotel sudo systemctl restart traefik-appmotel
sudo -u appmotel sudo systemctl status traefik-appmotel

Why this pattern? 1. sudo -u appmotel - Switch to appmotel user 2. sudo /bin/systemctl - appmotel uses its sudo permission to run systemctl as root

INCORRECT (will fail): 

# This fails because "apps" user doesn't have direct systemctl sudo access
sudo systemctl start traefik-appmotel

items.title: Viewing Traefik Logs
items.text:
The appmotel user has full access to Traefik logs for debugging:

# View recent logs
sudo -u appmotel sudo /usr/bin/journalctl -u traefik-appmotel -n 50

# View logs since a time
sudo -u appmotel sudo /usr/bin/journalctl -u traefik-appmotel --since "1 hour ago"

# Follow logs in real-time
sudo -u appmotel sudo /usr/bin/journalctl -u traefik-appmotel -f

# View logs without pager
sudo -u appmotel sudo /usr/bin/journalctl -u traefik-appmotel --no-pager

Note: The appmotel user can ONLY view traefik-appmotel logs. Attempting to view other service logs will be denied by sudoers.

items.title: Managing Application Services
items.text:
Application services run as user-level systemd services under the appmotel user.

# These commands don't need root - they use systemctl --user
sudo -u appmotel systemctl --user start appmotel-myapp
sudo -u appmotel systemctl --user stop appmotel-myapp
sudo -u appmotel systemctl --user status appmotel-myapp

# Or use the appmo CLI (preferred)
appmo start myapp
appmo stop myapp
appmo status myapp

items.title: Running General Commands as appmotel
items.text:
sudo -u appmotel whoami                           # Returns: appmotel
sudo -u appmotel bash /path/to/install.sh         # Run installation
appmo list                                        # appmo switches to appmotel by itself
appmo add myapp https://... main                  # Add an app

items.title: Required Permissions for appmotel User
items.text: The appmotel user requires the following permissions:

items.title: 1. Systemd Linger (Required)
items.text:
Allows user services to run without an active login session: 

sudo loginctl enable-linger appmotel

items.title: 2. Let's Encrypt Certificate Access (Required for HTTPS)
items.text:
Secure read access to TLS certificates using group-based permissions.

Background: The ssl-cert Convention

This follows the Debian/Ubuntu convention for secure certificate access: - Debian/Ubuntu: The ssl-cert package provides the ssl-cert group and /etc/ssl/private directory (mode 710) - RHEL/CentOS/Fedora: No such package exists; the group must be created manually - Purpose: Allows non-root services to read SSL/TLS private keys without making them world-readable

The Secure Approach (Recommended - Implemented by install.sh): 

# 1. Install ssl-cert package (Debian/Ubuntu only)
# On Debian/Ubuntu:
sudo apt-get install -y ssl-cert

# On RHEL/CentOS/Fedora, manually create the group:
sudo groupadd ssl-cert

# 2. Add appmotel user to ssl-cert group
sudo usermod -aG ssl-cert appmotel

# 3. Set group ownership
sudo chgrp -R ssl-cert /etc/letsencrypt/archive
sudo chgrp -R ssl-cert /etc/letsencrypt/live

# 4. Set secure permissions
# Directories: 750 (owner full, group read/execute, world none)
sudo chmod 750 /etc/letsencrypt/{archive,live}
sudo chmod 750 /etc/letsencrypt/archive/*
sudo chmod 750 /etc/letsencrypt/live/*

# 5. Private keys: 640 (owner read/write, group read, world none)
sudo find /etc/letsencrypt/archive -name "privkey*.pem" -exec chmod 640 {} \;

# 6. Public certs: 644 (standard for public certificates)
sudo find /etc/letsencrypt/archive -name "*.pem" ! -name "privkey*.pem" -exec chmod 644 {} \;

Why This Approach: - Security: Private keys are NOT readable by all users (prevents unauthorized access) - Access Control: Only members of ssl-cert group can access certificates - Standard Convention: - Debian/Ubuntu systems use the ssl-cert package which provides this group and /etc/ssl/private (mode 710) - RHEL/CentOS/Fedora don't have this package but the convention still applies - Manageable: Group membership can be managed centrally - Clean: Uses standard Unix permissions, no ACLs needed - Portable: Works across different Linux distributions - Much more secure than world-readable files (744) or overly permissive ACLs

Alternative (Not Recommended): 

# Using ACLs - works but less standard
sudo setfacl -R -m u:appmotel:rx /etc/letsencrypt/live/
sudo setfacl -R -m u:appmotel:rx /etc/letsencrypt/archive/

items.title: 3. CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (Handled by systemd)
items.text:
Traefik needs to bind ports 80 and 443. This is granted via the systemd service file: 

[Service]
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
PrivateUsers=no

Note: Do NOT set file capabilities on the Traefik binary (setcap). Use only systemd's AmbientCapabilities.

items.title: 4. Home Directory Structure
items.text:
The appmotel user needs these directories: 

/home/appmotel/
├── .config/
│   ├── appmotel/apps/          # App metadata
│   ├── systemd/user/           # User services
│   └── traefik/
│       ├── traefik.yaml        # Static config
│       └── dynamic/            # Dynamic configs (auto-watched)
├── .local/
│   ├── bin/                    # traefik, appmo binaries
│   └── share/
│       ├── appmotel/           # App repositories
│       └── traefik/acme.json   # ACME certificates (mode 600)
└── .bashrc                     # PATH includes ~/.local/bin

items.title: What appmotel CAN do:
items.text:
• Manage its own user-level systemd services
  • Start/stop/restart the Traefik system service (limited sudo)
  • Read Let's Encrypt certificates
  • Bind to privileged ports via Traefik (systemd capability)

items.title: What appmotel CANNOT do:
items.text:
• Run arbitrary commands as root
  • Install system packages
  • Modify system files
  • Access other users' home directories

items.title: Production vs Development
items.text:
For production, you may want to restrict the operator user's access:

# Production-only sudoers (more restrictive)
apps ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/su - appmotel
# Remove: apps ALL=(appmotel) NOPASSWD: ALL

This requires interactive shell for all appmotel operations but is more secure.

items.title: Testing the Configuration
items.text:
After configuring sudoers, verify:

# Test operator → appmotel delegation
sudo -u appmotel whoami
# Expected: appmotel

# Test appmotel → root (limited) delegation
sudo -u appmotel sudo systemctl status traefik-appmotel
# Expected: Shows Traefik service status

# Test that appmotel cannot run arbitrary root commands

# Expected: FAILS (not in allowed commands)

# Test user-level service management
sudo -u appmotel systemctl --user status
# Expected: Shows user services

items.title: Installation Flow
items.text:
Step 1: System-level setup (requires actual root): 

sudo bash install.sh

This creates: - The appmotel user - /etc/systemd/system/traefik-appmotel.service - /etc/sudoers.d/appmotel - Enables systemd linger

Step 2: User-level setup:

This installs: - Traefik binary - Configuration files - appmo CLI tool

items.title: Environment Variable Management
items.text: This guide explains how Appmotel manages .env files for application configuration.

items.title: Storage Location
items.text:
Physical .env files are stored in the config directory, NOT in the repository:

~/.config/appmotel/<app>/.env  # Physical file (persistent)
~/.local/share/appmotel/<app>/repo/.env  # Symlink to config file

This separation provides several benefits:

  1. Persistent configuration across app reinstalls and updates
  2. Security - Secrets never committed to git
  3. Backup/restore workflow - Configuration survives app removal
  4. Version control independence - Configuration changes don't affect git status

items.title: 1. Initial Deployment
items.text:
When you deploy an app with appmo add:

appmo add myapp https://github.com/username/repo main

Appmotel: 1. Clones the repository to ~/.local/share/appmotel/myapp/repo/ 2. Looks for a template in the app folder: .env.default, env.default, .env.example, env.example or .env.local (the first one found is copied). If there is none, an existing .env is moved. For a subfolder deploy, only the subfolder is searched, not the folders above it, so each app in a monorepo needs its own template. 3. Creates physical .env in ~/.config/appmotel/myapp/.env 4. Creates symlink from repo to config: repo/.env -> ~/.config/appmotel/myapp/.env 5. Assigns PORT if not specified (auto-assigned from 10001-59999)

items.title: 2. Editing Configuration
items.text:
Edit the .env file using the appmo env command:

appmo env myapp

This opens the physical file in ~/.config/appmotel/myapp/.env in vim (or vi), with the mouse off, so that you can select and paste text with your terminal. sudo drops $EDITOR, so vim is the usual editor.

To read or change one value without an editor (for scripts and agents):

appmo env myapp get DATABASE_URL          # prints the value; exit code 1 if it is not set
appmo env myapp set DEBUG false           # or: appmo env myapp set DEBUG=false
printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | appmo env myapp set API_TOKEN   # one value from stdin
appmo env myapp unset OLD_VAR OTHER_VAR   # remove variables
appmo env myapp set <<'EOF'               # many KEY=VALUE lines from stdin
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:pw@db/app
API_TOKEN=abc123
EOF
  • set replaces the line of the variable (and removes duplicate lines), or adds it at the end. It quotes the value if necessary.
  • set refuses names that are not valid, values with more than one line, and values that appmotel would skip when it loads the file ($(, backticks, ;, &&, ||).
  • Give secrets on stdin. A value on the command line is visible in the process list and in the sudo log, and set warns if the name looks like a secret (*PASS*, *TOKEN*, *KEY*, *SECRET* ...). The appmo audit log (journalctl -t appmo) hides the value in all forms.
  • With many lines on stdin, blank lines and # comments are skipped, and one pair of outer quotes is removed. If one line is refused, nothing is changed. Quote the here-doc marker (<<'EOF'), so that your shell does not expand $ in the values.
  • set does not restart the app. Run appmo restart myapp after the last change.

After editing, restart the app: 

appmo restart myapp

items.title: 3. Backup on Removal
items.text:
When you remove an app with appmo remove:

appmo remove myapp

Appmotel: 1. Stops all services for the app 2. Backs up .env to .env.backup in the same directory 3. Removes all services, configs, and repo 4. Preserves the backup for future restoration

items.title: 4. Restore on Re-add
items.text:
When re-adding a previously removed app:

appmo add myapp https://github.com/username/repo main

Appmotel detects the existing .env.backup and prompts:

Found previous .env backup for 'myapp'
Would you like to restore it? (y/n):
  • Yes: Restores the previous .env configuration
  • No: Creates fresh .env from repo template or defaults

items.title: Port Variable Detection
items.text: Appmotel supports multiple port variable names with priority order:

items.title: Priority Order
items.text:
1. PORT (highest priority)
  2. FLASK_PORT (for Flask apps)
  3. Any *PORT* variable (e.g., NODE_PORT, SERVER_PORT)

items.title: Reading Ports
items.text:
# Example .env file
PORT=8000
FLASK_PORT=8000

Appmotel reads ports using this logic: 

get_port_from_env() {
  # 1. Try PORT first
  port=$(grep -E '^PORT=' .env | cut -d'=' -f2)

  # 2. Fall back to FLASK_PORT
  port=$(grep -E '^FLASK_PORT=' .env | cut -d'=' -f2)

  # 3. Fall back to any *PORT* variable
  port=$(grep -iE '^[A-Z_]*PORT[A-Z_]*=' .env | cut -d'=' -f2)
}

items.title: Updating Ports
items.text:
When Appmotel assigns or updates ports, it updates both PORT and FLASK_PORT if they exist:

# Before
PORT=5000
FLASK_PORT=5000

# After appmo assigns port 8123
PORT=8123
FLASK_PORT=8123

items.title: Environment Variable Precedence
items.text:
When an app runs, environment variables come from these sources (highest to lowest priority):

  1. Systemd service Environment= directives (e.g., PORT)
  2. .env file in app's config directory
  3. System environment (inherited from systemd user session)
  4. Application defaults (hardcoded in app code)

Appmotel injects critical variables directly into the systemd service: 

[Service]
Environment="PORT=8000"
EnvironmentFile=%h/.config/appmotel/myapp/.env

This ensures PORT is always available, even if .env is missing.

.env

items.title: Dynamic Configuration with Scripts
items.text:
Use install.sh to generate configuration:

install.sh: 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

# Generate random secrets if not already set
env_file=~/.config/appmotel/myapp/.env

if ! grep -q "^SECRET_KEY=" "${env_file}" 2>/dev/null; then
  secret=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
  echo "SECRET_KEY=${secret}" >> "${env_file}"
  echo "Generated new SECRET_KEY"
fi

if ! grep -q "^JWT_SECRET=" "${env_file}" 2>/dev/null; then
  jwt=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
  echo "JWT_SECRET=${jwt}" >> "${env_file}"
  echo "Generated new JWT_SECRET"
fi

This automatically generates secrets on first deployment while preserving them on updates.

items.title: Isolated Apps
items.text: This page is for the sysadmin who runs an appmotel server. Read it before you put apps with secrets on a shared server.

items.title: The problem
items.text:
By default, every app runs as the same Linux user, appmotel. So every app can read the files of every other app:

  • the .env files of all apps (database passwords, API keys, tokens)
  • appmotel's own .env (for example AWS keys for Route53)
  • the TLS private keys in acme.json
  • appmotel's GitHub SSH key

If one app has a bug that lets an attacker run code or read files, the attacker gets the secrets of all apps on the server.

items.title: The solution: one Linux user for each app
items.text:
An isolated app runs as its own Linux user, a-<app>. For example, the app billing runs as a-billing.

appmo add --isolated billing user/billing-repo        # new app
appmo isolate billing                                 # existing app

All other commands stay the same. appmo start, stop, restart, update, logs, env, exec, status, check, backup, restore, backups, remove, list and autopull work for isolated apps too.

items.title: What an isolated app cannot do
items.text:
Attempt by the app user Result Read appmotel's .env, or the .env of another app Permission denied Read acme.json (TLS keys) or the Traefik config Permission denied Read the home of another app user Permission denied Use sudo, or become appmotel Refused, the user has no sudo rights Change Traefik routes (for example, take over the host name of another app) Not possible, only appmotel writes routes Run appmo self-update or appmo isolate Refused

All of these were tested on a real server.

items.title: What isolation does NOT protect
items.text:
• Network: app ports are closed to other machines (appmotel-firewall.service). On the server itself, an app user may open connections only to its own app port. To reach another app, it must go through Traefik (https://<app>.<BASE_DOMAIN>), with its rate limits. Normal (not isolated) apps run as appmotel and can still reach each other. The rule is in the nft table inet appmotel (chain output, sets app_uids and own_ports); the root helper appmotel-user firewall fills the sets from the app users and their ports. appmo refuses a PORT that another app already uses.
  • CPU and memory: isolated apps share the machine. MEMORY_LIMIT and CPU_QUOTA still apply per app.
  • appmotel itself: whoever controls appmotel (or the operator user, apps by default) controls all isolated apps too. This is by design.
  • Private repos: see Private repos and SSH keys.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
operator (apps) --sudo--> appmotel --sudo -u a-<app>--> a-<app>
                             |                             |
                         Traefik routes,             app files, venv,
                         isolated.conf               systemd user service
  • The app user: a-<app>, with its own home /home/a-<app> (mode 700), member of the group appmotel-apps. Linger is on, so its systemd user services run without a login.
  • The root helper /usr/local/bin/appmotel-user: creates and deletes app users. appmotel may run it with sudo. The helper:
  • accepts only valid app names (at most 30 characters)
  • never takes over a user that it did not create
  • refuses to finish if the new user would get any sudo rights
  • The control path: /etc/sudoers.d/appmotel-a-<app> contains one line, appmotel ALL=(a-<app>) NOPASSWD: ALL. So appmotel can run anything as that user, and nothing in the other direction.
  • The operator rules: the rules in /etc/sudoers.d/appmotel for the operators (appmotel-ops, OPERATOR_USERS) and for the group appmotel-users exclude the app users, <operators>, !%appmotel-apps. This also holds when OPERATOR_USERS=ALL, or when an app user is put into appmotel-users by mistake.
  • Two roles of appmo: run as appmotel, it is in admin role. Run as an a-* user, it is in app role: it manages only the apps in that user's home, never switches to appmotel, and never writes Traefik config.
  • What appmotel keeps: for an isolated app, appmotel keeps only ~/.config/appmotel/<app>/isolated.conf (the user and the port). For each command, appmo runs itself as the app user. After the command, appmotel rebuilds the Traefik route from the app's port and .env. It checks every value first, so a changed .env cannot add routes for other host names.

items.title: Where the files are
items.text: What Normal app Isolated app Repo, venv /home/appmotel/.local/share/appmotel/<app>/repo /home/a-<app>/.local/share/appmotel/<app>/repo .env, metadata /home/appmotel/.config/appmotel/<app>/ /home/a-<app>/.config/appmotel/<app>/ systemd unit /home/appmotel/.config/systemd/user/ /home/a-<app>/.config/systemd/user/ Backups /home/appmotel/.local/share/appmotel-backups/<app>/ /home/a-<app>/.local/share/appmotel-backups/<app>/ Traefik route /home/appmotel/.config/traefik/dynamic/<app>.yaml same (written by appmotel)

items.title: Upgrading an existing server
items.text:
Do this once, from a checkout of the new appmotel version.

  1. Run the system part as root. It creates the groups appmotel-apps, appmotel-users and appmotel-ops, installs /usr/local/bin/appmotel-user and writes the new sudoers rules: 
    sudo bash install.sh
  2. Run the user part as appmotel. It sets the new file modes and installs uv: 
    sudo -u appmotel bash install.sh
  3. Check the result: 
    sudo cat /etc/sudoers.d/appmotel | grep appmotel-apps     # the exclusion is there
sudo -u apps cat /home/appmotel/.config/appmotel/.env      # must say: Permission denied

Existing apps keep working unchanged. Move them one at a time with appmo isolate <app>.

Changed behaviour after the upgrade:

  • appmotel's ~/.config, data and backup folders are now mode 700, and all .env files mode 600. Before, any local user could read them. Scripts that read these files directly as another user (for example as apps) must now use sudo -u appmotel cat ... or appmo exec <app> cat .env.
  • Tab completion of app names no longer works for the operator user, for the same reason.
  • appmo list has a new USER column.

items.title: Moving an app: appmo isolate
items.text:
appmo isolate <app>:

  1. Makes a backup of the app.
  2. Creates the user and stops the old services.
  3. Copies the repo into the new home, together with files that git does not track (for example SQLite databases or uploads). Venvs are not copied; they are built again.
  4. Copies the app's .env.
  5. Deploys the app as the new user on the same port and moves the route.

The URL stays the same. If any step fails, appmotel deletes the new user, restores the old route and starts the old services again.

The app is down while it is built again. That is a few seconds for small apps, about 1 to 2 minutes for a Next.js build.

The backup from step 1 stays in appmotel's backup folder, and isolate prints its path. appmo restore cannot use it after the move, because restore now runs as the app user. To go back to the old app: run appmo remove <app>, add the app again without --isolated, and copy the .env from that backup.

items.title: Private repos and SSH keys
items.text:
The app user has no GitHub access of its own.

  • Public repo: appmotel clones it over HTTPS. No key is copied.
  • Private repo: appmotel copies its own GitHub SSH key into /home/a-<app>/.ssh/. The app user can then read every repo that this key can read, not only its own. If that is not acceptable, use a separate deploy key for each repo. Until appmo supports that, you can put a deploy key in /home/a-<app>/.ssh/ yourself and remove the copied key.

appmotel treats a repo as private when the GitHub API does not show it as public.

items.title: Removing an isolated app
items.text:
appmo remove <app> does these things:

  • stops the app
  • keeps its .env as /home/appmotel/.config/appmotel/<app>/.env.backup, which the next appmo add of that name restores
  • saves the app's backups as one archive in /home/appmotel/.local/share/appmotel-backups/
  • deletes the user, its home and its sudoers file

items.title: Python versions (uv)
items.text:
Each app user can have its own Python version. If an app asks for a version, appmotel builds the venv with uv. uv installs that Python into the app user's home, so no root and no system package is needed. About 90 MB of disk is used for each app that does this.

The version is taken from the first of these that is set:

  1. PYTHON_VERSION=3.12 in the app's .env
  2. a .python-version file in the repo
  3. requires-python in pyproject.toml
  4. PYTHON_VERSION in appmotel's .env (the default for all apps)

If none is set, the system python3 is used, as before.

To change the version of a deployed app, set PYTHON_VERSION in its .env and remove the old venv:

appmo env myapp                       # add PYTHON_VERSION=3.12
appmo exec myapp rm -rf .venv
appmo update myapp

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
appmo list                                     # USER column shows a-<app> for isolated apps
appmo logs myapp                               # logs of the app user's service
sudo -u appmotel sudo -u a-myapp bash -l       # a shell as the app user (as operator)
sudo -l -U a-myapp                             # must say: not allowed to run sudo
  • "Could not create user a-myapp": /usr/local/bin/appmotel-user is missing or old. Run sudo bash install.sh.
  • "user a-myapp would get sudo rights": an old operator rule in /etc/sudoers.d/appmotel has no !%appmotel-apps exclusion. Run sudo bash install.sh.
  • The URL gives 404 for a moment after a deploy: Traefik loads a new route about a second after it is written. appmo add waits for the URL before it ends.

items.title: Multi-Component Applications
items.text: Appmotel automatically detects and deploys applications with multiple service components (e.g., frontend + backend) as a unified app.

items.title: Supported Directory Structure
items.text: Appmotel recognizes multi-component apps in two layouts:

items.title: Root-Level Components
items.text:
myapp/
├── frontend/
│   ├── package.json
│   └── ...
├── backend/
│   ├── requirements.txt
│   └── ...
└── .env

items.title: Src Subdirectory Components
items.text:
myapp/
├── src/
│   ├── frontend/
│   │   ├── package.json
│   │   └── ...
│   └── backend/
│       ├── requirements.txt
│       └── ...
└── .env

items.title: Recognized Component Names
items.text:
Appmotel automatically detects these component directory names:

  • frontend/ - Web frontend (React, Vue, Next.js, etc.)
  • backend/ - Application backend/API
  • api/ - API server
  • worker/ - Background worker/queue processor
  • db/ - Database component
  • cache/ - Cache service

items.title: Service Naming Convention
items.text:
Each component becomes a systemd service with specific naming:

  • Frontend: appmotel-<app>.service (no suffix)
  • Gets the public PORT
  • Exposed via Traefik HTTPS

  • Accessible at https://<app>.apps.yourdomain.edu

  • Backend: appmotel-<app>-backend.service

  • Gets an internal port (not publicly accessible)

  • Other components connect via localhost

  • Other Components: appmotel-<app>-{component}.service

  • Each gets an internal port
  • Not publicly accessible

items.title: Port Allocation
items.text:
• Frontend: Receives the main PORT from .env (or auto-assigned 10001-59999)
  • Backend/Other: Automatically assigned sequential internal ports
  • All components can communicate via localhost

items.title: Directory Structure
items.text:
myshop/
├── frontend/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── next.config.js
│   └── ...
├── backend/
│   ├── requirements.txt
│   ├── app.py
│   └── ...
├── .env
└── install.sh

items.title: .env File
items.text:
PORT=8000
APP_NAME="MyShop"
MEMORY_LIMIT=512M
CPU_QUOTA=100%

items.title: install.sh
items.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

echo "Installing MyShop components..."

# Frontend setup
if [[ -d frontend ]]; then
  cd frontend
  npm install
  npm run build
  cd ..
fi

# Backend setup
if [[ -d backend ]]; then
  cd backend
  python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
  cd ..
fi

echo "Installation complete"

items.title: Deployment
items.text:
Deploy multi-component apps the same way as single-component apps:

# Deploy from GitHub
appmo add myshop https://github.com/username/myshop main

# Deploy from subfolder
appmo add myshop https://github.com/username/monorepo/tree/main/apps/myshop

Appmotel will: 1. Detect both frontend/ and backend/ directories 2. Create two systemd services 3. Assign ports appropriately 4. Configure Traefik to route to frontend only

items.title: Service Management
items.text:
All appmo commands affect ALL services in the app namespace:

# Check status (shows all components)
appmo status myshop
# Output:
# myshop (frontend): active
# myshop-backend: active

# Restart all components
appmo restart myshop
# Restarts both frontend and backend

# View logs (shows all components)
appmo logs myshop

# Stop all components
appmo stop myshop

# Remove all components
appmo remove myshop

items.title: Unified App View
items.text:
Multi-component apps appear as a single app in listings:

$ appmo list
myshop      https://myshop.apps.yourdomain.edu    active
otherapp    https://otherapp.apps.yourdomain.edu  active

Use appmo status to see individual component details:

$ appmo status myshop
App: myshop
URL: https://myshop.apps.yourdomain.edu
Branch: main
Status: active

Services:
  appmotel-myshop (frontend): active (running)
  appmotel-myshop-backend: active (running)

items.title: Component Communication
items.text:
Components can communicate via localhost using their assigned ports:

Frontend Environment (automatically available): 

PORT=8000                    # Frontend's public port
BACKEND_PORT=8001            # Backend's internal port (example)

Example: Frontend connecting to backend 

// In your frontend code (e.g., Next.js API route)
const backendUrl = `http://localhost:${process.env.BACKEND_PORT || 8001}/api`;
const response = await fetch(`${backendUrl}/users`);

items.title: Component Requirements
items.text:
Each component must have:

  1. App type identifier (one of):
  2. Python: requirements.txt or pyproject.toml
  3. Node.js: package.json with start script
  4. Go: go.mod

  5. Custom: start.sh

  6. Proper port binding:

  7. Read PORT environment variable
  8. Bind to 0.0.0.0 or localhost
  9. Use high ports (10001-59999)

items.title: Automatic Framework Support
items.text: Appmotel provides automatic build and serve for common frameworks:

items.title: Next.js Static Export (Frontend)
items.text:
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "next build",
    "start": "next start"
  }
}

If next.config.js has output: 'export', Appmotel: 1. Runs npm run build 2. Serves the out/ directory with serve 3. Auto-configures the start script

items.title: Vite + TypeScript (Frontend)
items.text:
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "start": "vite preview"
  }
}

Appmotel: 1. Runs npm run build 2. Serves the dist/ directory with serve 3. Auto-configures the start script

items.title: Python with Virtual Environment (Backend)
items.text: If start.sh exists, Appmotel: 1. Creates virtual environment in .venv/ 2. Installs dependencies 3. Automatically adds .venv/bin to PATH

App: ecommerce
URL: https://ecommerce.apps.yourdomain.edu
Services:
  appmotel-ecommerce (frontend): active
  appmotel-ecommerce-api: active
  appmotel-ecommerce-worker: active

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
1. Keep components independent: Each component should be deployable separately
  2. Use environment variables: Pass configuration via .env file
  3. Implement health checks: Add /health endpoint to each component
  4. Log to stdout/stderr: Systemd captures all output automatically
  5. Test locally first: Verify component communication on localhost before deploying

# Clean the appmotel user's home directory
cd /path/to/appmotel
sudo -u appmotel bash bin/reset-home.sh --force

# Run installation
sudo bash install.sh

items.text: Run these with one normal and one isolated app (appmo add --isolated). bash tests/test-appmo.sh covers the parsing and file generation; these steps cover the parts that need a real host.

items.title: Rollback and Pin
items.text:
appmo backups flask-hello                 # COMMIT column is filled
# push a commit that breaks the app, wait for autopull (or appmo update flask-hello)
appmo rollback flask-hello                # back to the commit before the push
appmo status flask-hello                  # "Pinned: rolled back to <commit>"
journalctl --user -u appmotel-autopull -n 5   # "... (1 pinned by rollback, not updated)"
appmo backups flask-hello                 # a new backup of the broken state (undo with appmo restore)
appmo unpin flask-hello                   # next autopull deploys the branch again

Expected: the app runs the old commit and autopull does not touch it until unpin. A second appmo rollback goes one version further back. appmo update also removes the pin.

items.title: Scheduled Jobs
items.text:
# in the app repo
printf '*:0/2 | date >> /tmp/job-test.log\nbogus | true\n' > examples/flask-hello/appmo-schedule
# push, then wait for autopull
appmo status flask-hello                  # "Scheduled jobs": 1 timer, next run in < 2 min
appmo logs flask-hello --grep 'scheduled job'   # the timer ran it
appmo stop flask-hello                    # timer stops too; appmo start resumes it

Expected: the bogus line is skipped with a WARN at deploy time. Removing the file and pushing removes the timer; appmo remove removes it too.

items.title: Restart Limit and Crash Loop
items.text:
appmo env flask-hello set RESTART_LIMIT 3
appmo restart flask-hello                 # writes appmotel-flask-hello.service.d/restart-limit.conf
# push a commit whose app exits at start (raise SystemExit(1) at the top of app.py), wait for autopull
sleep 60; appmo status flask-hello        # "FAILED: crash loop, systemd stopped restarting it"
# next autopull run: ERROR "flask-hello: crash loop ..." (and a webhook message if set)
appmo rollback flask-hello                # running again on the good commit
appmo env flask-hello unset RESTART_LIMIT; appmo restart flask-hello   # drop-in removed

Without RESTART_LIMIT, appmo status shows CRASHED, systemd restarts it and autopull still reports the crash loop (3+ restarts between two runs).

items.title: TLS Certificates
items.text: Every app gets HTTPS at https://<app>.BASE_DOMAIN. You do not have to issue or renew a certificate for each app yourself. appmotel uses one of two sources, in this order.

items.title: 1. A wildcard certificate that you supply (certbot)
items.text:
If /etc/letsencrypt/live/<name>/ holds a certificate for exactly *.BASE_DOMAIN, appmotel uses it for all apps.

  • install.sh finds it and writes ~/.config/traefik/dynamic/tls-config.yaml, which makes it Traefik's default certificate. App routes then use tls: {}.
  • A certificate for a different domain is never used. For example, with BASE_DOMAIN=apps.example.edu, a certificate for *.other.example.edu or *.example.edu is ignored. (*.example.edu does not cover x.apps.example.edu, because a wildcard covers only one label.)
  • appmotel must be able to read the key. install.sh gives the ssl-cert group read access, and /usr/local/bin/appmotel-fix-certs does it again after a change.
  • Renewal is certbot's job. install.sh installs a certbot deploy hook that restarts Traefik after a renewal, because Traefik reads these files only once at start.
  • appmo autopull warns in the log 14 days before the certificate expires (TLS_EXPIRY_WARN_DAYS).

To issue such a wildcard yourself, certbot needs the DNS-01 challenge, for example:

sudo certbot certonly --dns-route53 -d '*.apps.example.edu'
sudo bash install.sh      # picks up the new certificate

items.title: 2. Let's Encrypt through Traefik (ACME)
items.text:
If there is no matching wildcard certificate and USE_LETSENCRYPT=yes, Traefik gets certificates from Let's Encrypt by itself:

  • For each app route, Traefik asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate for that host name the first time a client connects. This takes a few seconds; until then, Traefik's default certificate is served.
  • Traefik renews each certificate about 30 days before it expires. No cron job and no restart is needed.
  • All certificates and the ACME account key are in ~/.local/share/traefik/acme.json (mode 600, only appmotel can read it).
  • A new app gets its certificate without any manual step. Removed apps keep their old certificate in acme.json until it expires; that is harmless.

You select how Let's Encrypt checks that you control the domain with LETSENCRYPT_MODE:

LETSENCRYPT_MODE How Let's Encrypt checks Needs http (default) It fetches a token from http://<app>.BASE_DOMAIN/.well-known/acme-challenge/ on port 80 Port 80 open from the internet dns Traefik writes a TXT record in Route53 Route53 zone, AWS credentials or an EC2 instance role. No inbound port is needed

What you get depends on the mode. Let's Encrypt issues wildcard certificates only with the DNS-01 challenge:

  • http: one certificate for each app host name. A new app has Traefik's default certificate for a few seconds, until its own certificate arrives.
  • dns: one wildcard certificate, *.BASE_DOMAIN plus BASE_DOMAIN, for all apps. Every app route asks for the same certificate, and Traefik gets it only once. A new app has a valid certificate at once.

items.title: DNS mode (Route53)
items.text:
Traefik needs Route53 access, from an EC2 instance role or from AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in the .env. The role needs route53:ListHostedZonesByName, route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets and route53:GetChange.

Route53 is a global service, but the AWS SDK in Traefik needs a region. If AWS_REGION is not set, install.sh adds AWS_REGION="us-east-1" to the .env.

The first wildcard can take about 3 minutes, because Let's Encrypt waits until the TXT record is visible.

Switching an existing server from http to dns: set LETSENCRYPT_MODE="dns" and run appmo self-update. This rebuilds all app routes, and new apps get the wildcard. Existing apps keep their own certificates, because Traefik prefers a certificate for the exact host name. To move all apps to the wildcard at once, move the old certificates away:

sudo -u appmotel mv /home/appmotel/.local/share/traefik/acme.json /home/appmotel/.local/share/traefik/acme.json.old
sudo -u appmotel sudo systemctl restart traefik-appmotel

Until the wildcard arrives (about 3 minutes), clients see Traefik's default certificate. Do it at a quiet time.

items.title: Turned on by default for new installs
items.text:
When install.sh creates a new ~/.config/appmotel/.env and finds no matching wildcard certificate, it sets USE_LETSENCRYPT=yes if:

  • no other program listens on port 80, and
  • ufw or firewalld, if active, allows port 80.

The server cannot test the firewalls outside the machine (for example an AWS security group or a campus firewall). If they block port 80, Traefik only logs failed attempts and serves its default certificate. Open port 80, or use LETSENCRYPT_MODE=dns.

An existing .env is never changed. To turn Let's Encrypt on later:

sudo -u appmotel nano /home/appmotel/.config/appmotel/.env
#   USE_LETSENCRYPT=yes
#   LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL=""         # optional (example.com addresses are rejected)
#   LETSENCRYPT_MODE="http"      # or "dns"
appmo self-update

items.title: Rate limits
items.text: Let's Encrypt allows 50 new certificates for each registered domain per week. In http mode each app uses one, which is enough for most servers. If you add and remove many apps, use dns mode or a wildcard certificate from section 1.

items.title: Check which certificate an app gets
items.text:
echo | openssl s_client -connect myapp.apps.example.edu:443 -servername myapp.apps.example.edu 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject -dates
Issuer Meaning O=Let's Encrypt and subject CN=*.apps.example.edu Your certbot wildcard certificate (section 1) O=Let's Encrypt and subject CN=apps.example.edu Traefik's wildcard certificate in dns mode (section 2) O=Let's Encrypt and subject CN=myapp.apps.example.edu Traefik's certificate for this app in http mode (section 2) CN=TRAEFIK DEFAULT CERT No certificate yet. Wait a few seconds (DNS-01: up to 3 minutes), then look at the Traefik log. Traefik does not retry a failed order by itself, so autopull restarts Traefik when it still serves this certificate 10 minutes after it started (at most once an hour) 
sudo journalctl -u traefik-appmotel -n 50 | grep -i acme

items.title: Appmotel Example Applications
items.text: This directory contains sample applications that demonstrate how to structure apps for Appmotel deployment.

items.title: 1. Flask Hello World (flask-hello/)
items.text:
A simple Python Flask web application.

Files: - app.py - Main Flask application - requirements.txt - Python dependencies - .env - Environment variables - install.sh - Installation script

Deploy: 

cd flask-hello
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
# Push to GitHub and deploy with appmo

items.title: 2. Express Hello World (express-hello/)
items.text:
A simple Node.js Express web application.

Files: - server.js - Main Express application - package.json - Node.js dependencies and start script - .env - Environment variables - install.sh - Installation script

Deploy: 

cd express-hello
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
# Push to GitHub and deploy with appmo

items.title: 3. Zensical Wiki (zensical-wiki/)
items.text:
A documentation site built with Zensical. No server code needed: Appmotel detects zensical.toml, installs Zensical into .venv, runs zensical build, and serves the generated site/ directory.

Files: - zensical.toml - Site configuration - docs/ - Markdown content

Deploy: 

appmo add zensical-test https://github.com/dirkpetersen/appmotel/tree/main/examples/zensical-wiki

A brand-new zensical new project deploys the same way. Set site_url in zensical.toml to the app's URL (the scaffold's example.com placeholder only affects canonical links and sitemap.xml). Add a requirements.txt to pin the Zensical version or install extensions.

items.title: Creating Your Own Application
items.text:
Your application must include:

  1. .env file - Environment configuration 

    PORT=8000  # Optional, will be auto-assigned if not specified
# Add your custom environment variables

  2. install.sh - Installation script (optional) 

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -o errexit
set -o nounset
set -o pipefail

echo "Running installation tasks..."
# Add your installation logic here

  3. Application files:

  4. Python: requirements.txt + app.py (or single .py file)
  5. Node.js: package.json with scripts.start defined
  6. Custom: Executable in bin/ directory

items.title: Testing Locally
items.text:
Before deploying to Appmotel, test your app locally:

Python: 

cd flask-hello
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python3 app.py

Node.js: 

cd express-hello
npm install
npm start

Visit http://localhost:<PORT> to verify your app works.
